title: Problem-Driven Innovation in Genome Editing: From Programmable Nucleases to DSB-Free Precision Editors and the Path to Clinical Translation.

abstract: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) is a group of rare autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiencies characterized by impaired leukocyte migration resulting from defective expression or function of adhesion molecules. The most common and severe form, LAD-I, is caused by biallelic mutations in Integrin Subunit Beta 2 (ITGB2), which encodes the β2-integrin subunit CD18, leading to recurrent life-threatening infections and impaired wound healing. LAD-II arises from mutations in the fucose-metabolism gene SLC35C1, and LAD-III from mutations in FERMT3, which disrupt integrin activation through kindlin-3. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has historically been the only established curative treatment for severe LAD-I, but donor availability, conditioning toxicity, and graft-versus-host disease limit its use and have motivated the development of autologous approaches. Autologous gene therapy using self-inactivating lentiviral vectors to introduce functional ITGB2 into patient-derived hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells has shown promising clinical results, including restored CD18 expression, improved leukocyte function, and fewer severe infections. In March 2026, the FDA granted accelerated approval to marnetegragene autotemcel (Kresladi; RP-L201), making it the first approved gene therapy for severe LAD-I in the United States. CRISPR/Cas9, base editing, and prime editing are also being investigated as alternative approaches for correcting ITGB2 mutations, although their application in LAD-I remains preclinical. These methods could allow correction of pathogenic ITGB2 variants without relying on integrating viral vectors, but their efficacy and long-term safety in LAD-I have yet to be established. However, conditioning-related toxicity, the need for long-term safety monitoring, and the complexity and cost of manufacturing remain important limitations to wider clinical use. This review examines the molecular basis of LAD, preclinical and clinical studies of gene therapy for LAD-I, and the challenges that remain in translating genome-editing approaches into clinical practice.

title: Gene Therapy for Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type I: Current Advances, Clinical Translation, and Future Perspectives.

abstract: Due to the increasing demand for clinical gene therapy and the limitations of current treatment methods, there is an urgent need to develop gene-editing tools that are safer, more precise, and more clinically implementable. Deaminase-based base editors have emerged as gene-editing platforms with significant therapeutic potential because they can achieve precise single-base substitutions without inducing DNA double-strand breaks. However, the challenges of applying base editing in clinical practice extend beyond whether the intended edit can be achieved. The critical question is whether the editing system can reliably provide predictable, controllable, and verifiable outcomes across complex sequence contexts, diverse cell environments, and actual delivery conditions. This review focuses on the engineering optimization and clinical translation of base editors. We first systematically analyze the major factors affecting the clinical translation of base editors across four dimensions: editing efficiency, editing precision, safety, and delivery, together with the corresponding optimization strategies. We then summarize the applications of artificial intelligence and computational approaches in base editor design, screening, and risk assessment. We further discuss the ex vivo and in vivo pathways for clinical translation, including their respective requirements for product quality and safety evaluation. Finally, based on representative clinical programs, we discuss how editing performance, safety, and delivery factors influence development decisions for candidate base-editing systems across different therapeutic contexts, and propose minimum reporting recommendations to improve the consistency of key data and cross-study comparability.

title: From off-target to on-demand: Precision engineering and translational evaluation of next-generation base editors.

abstract: Following the rapid development and global deployment of messenger RNA vaccines, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) emerged as a pivotal nonviral platform for nucleic acid therapy. Rising fund support has driven rapid progress in LNP research in China, resulting in a visible increase in research output and clinical pipelines over the past five years. These studies developed optimized LNPs for the delivery of various genetic cargos, covering a broad application scope from prophylactic vaccines to in vivo cell therapy. In this review, we summarize the preclinical and clinical progress of LNP-enabled nucleic acid therapy in China and provide perspectives to tackle the challenges for clinical translation.

title: Preclinical and Clinical Advances in Lipid Nanoparticle-Enabled Nucleic Acid Therapy in China.

abstract: Newcastle disease virus (NDV or AOaV-1) is an avian paramyxovirus that typically causes only mild, self-limiting disease in humans. Here, we report fatal neuroinvasive AOaV-1 infection in a patient with multiple myeloma receiving maintenance therapy with teclistamab, daratumumab, and lenalidomide following frontline teclistamab-based treatment and autologous stem cell transplantation. Following rapidly progressive brainstem-cerebellar encephalitis and negative conventional microbiological testing, unbiased metagenomic RNA sequencing of a cerebellar biopsy identified AOaV-1 at high intraparenchymal abundance. Viral genome analysis revealed striking A-to-G and U-to-C substitutions selectively concentrated in the matrix gene, consistent with ADAR-mediated RNA editing. Long-read sequencing resolved two genetically distinct, independently hypermutated CNS haplotypes. Post-mortem analysis demonstrated widespread dissemination and continued viral diversification in multiple brain regions, whereas a peripheral urine sample contained a minimally mutated putative ancestral lineage. These findings support peripheral infection followed by CNS seeding and compartmentalized within-host evolution. The selective matrix-gene hypermutation closely parallels persistent measles virus infection in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, revealing a shared mechanism of paramyxovirus adaptation to the CNS. Profound immunotherapy-associated immune dysfunction may thus create niches enabling normally low-pathogenic zoonotic viruses to persist, evolve, and acquire severe neurovirulence.

title: Measles-like hypermutation of a Newcastle disease virus drives fatal encephalitis during BCMA × CD3 T-cell-redirecting immunotherapy.

abstract: Cancer remains a leading global mortality cause, driven by complex interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) that facilitate progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Cytokines form the central regulatory network governing TME intercellular communication, exerting highly context-dependent pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects. Dysregulated cytokine signaling drives chronic inflammation and immunosuppression, limiting durable therapeutic responses. While cytokine-based immunotherapies show clinical potential, their widespread use is hindered by poor stability, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and dose-limiting toxicities. Advances in nanomedicine offer innovative solutions by improving cytokine pharmacokinetics, tumor-selective delivery, and spatiotemporally controlled release. Beyond passive delivery, engineered nanoplatforms act as active modulators of the tumor immune ecosystem, remodeling cytokine networks to restore antitumor immunity. Nanotechnology interventions effectively regulate key signaling pathways- including JAK/STAT, TGF-β/SMAD, NF-κB, MAPK/ERK, and PI3K/AKT- disrupting pathological feedback mechanisms and crosstalk. Furthermore, localized cytokine delivery, gene silencing, mRNA therapeutics, and CRISPR-enabled genome engineering are expanding precision immunotherapy. Despite significant translational challenges such as tumor heterogeneity, biological barriers, immunogenicity, and manufacturing complexity emerging biomimetic and personalized nanoplatforms offer promising avenues for precise immune modulation and biomarker-guided patient stratification. Literature searches were conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect (with Google Scholar for citation tracking) covering peer-reviewed publications from 2003 to 2026.

title: Cytokine networks in the tumor microenvironment: nanotherapeutic modulation of immune-cell communication and signaling networks.

abstract: Joubert Syndrome (JBTS) is a ciliopathy and disease-causing variants in CEP290 are the leading cause of JBTS presenting with cerebello-retinal-renal phenotypes. We investigated a Brazilian child with JBTS and compound heterozygous variants in CEP290. Using patient derived fibroblasts, we characterised the c.6271-8T>G intron 46 splice site allele using RT-PCR, confirming it led to a 7 bp intronic inclusion leading to a frameshift and downstream nonsense variant p.(Asn2091Leufs*12). Patient fibroblasts displayed elongated and tortuous primary cilia and a decreased primary ciliation rate. We reviewed other Brazilian cohorts where the CEP290 c.6271-8T>G allele had been reported in homozygosity or in compound heterozygosity with a second pathogenic variant. Phenotypes associated with this allele included Leber congenital amaurosis, nephronophthisis and JBTS. Finally, we used antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) mediated exon skipping of exon 46, an 87 base pair exon which if skipped is not predicted to disrupt reading frame or CEP290 protein structure, in patient fibroblasts to rescue ciliary phenotypes and CEP290 protein expression at ciliary the transition zone. These findings confirm that the CEP290 c.6271-8T>G is a pathogenic splice-site variant and pathogenic alleles within or disrupting exon 46 splicing including c.6271-8T>G are amenable to targeted ASO mediated exon skipping as a future therapeutic strategy.

title: Targeted antisense oligonucleotide mediated exon skipping therapies for a recurrent CEP290 mutation.

abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and related cancers remain significant public health concerns worldwide. Among high-risk HPV genotypes, HPV16 demonstrates the highest epidemiological prevalence. The viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 are crucial drivers of HPV16-associated carcinogenesis and have become key therapeutic targets for treating HPV16-related cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cancers. HPV prophylactic vaccines have been widely implemented in clinical practice; however, effective therapeutic interventions for infected individuals remain limited. Therefore, the development of therapeutic HPV vaccines is urgently needed. LY01620 is an investigational mRNA therapeutic vaccine targeting HPV16 E6/E7 antigens. To support LY01620's clinical trial application and development, comprehensive nonclinical studies were conducted, including immunogenicity evaluations in mice and rats, anti-tumor activity and mechanistic studies in C3.43 tumor-bearing mice, single-dose tissue distribution study in rats, and a GLP-compliant repeated-dose toxicity study in rats combined with toxicokinetics, local irritation, and immunotoxicity assessments. LY01620 demonstrated strong immunogenicity in mice and rats and exhibited significant anti-tumor activity through inducing a strong Th1-polarized immune response, increasing frequency of antigen-specific T cells, and enhancing infiltration of CD8+ T cells and mature macrophages into tumors. LY01620 mRNA exhibited sustained accumulation in inguinal lymph nodes and spleens, potentially facilitating persistent antigen presentation and prolonged immunological effects. In the repeated-dose toxicity study in SD rats, LY01620 exhibited a favorable safety profile, with the no observed adverse effect level was the highest dose of 300 μg/animal. In conclusion, preclinical studies have demonstrated that LY01620 exhibited favorable mechanism of action-related efficacy and a well-tolerated safety profile, supporting its further development.

title: Nonclinical pharmacology and toxicology studies of LY01620, a therapeutic mRNA vaccine against human papillomavirus 16-related cancers.

abstract: The application of mRNA-based medicines, such as SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, has expanded to gene therapy and therapeutic protein delivery. RNA products by in vitro transcription (IVT) are intrinsically heterogeneous, comprising short, long, and incompletely processed transcripts. Because the 5' cap and 3' poly(A) tail act synergistically to support intracellular mRNA stability and efficient translation, preserving structural integrity across the entire transcript is a critical quality attribute for therapeutic mRNA manufacturing. Therefore, we established an integrated production workflow for producing structurally defined Cap2 mRNA while preserving structural integrity across the entire transcript. A 4.1-kb mRNA model is transcribed using a hydrophobic-tagged Cap2 analog. Ion-pair reversed-phase HPLC enriches the tagged Cap2 transcripts and purges any uncapped species and dsRNA impurities. An intermediate in-line UV-A photocleavage process is applied to photodecage and restore cap structure. Subsequent oligo(dT) affinity chromatography selectively isolates poly(A)-containing transcripts, enabling sequential enrichment of both terminal structural elements: the 5' cap and 3' poly(A) tail. The final product consisted almost entirely of capped transcripts, exhibited enhanced size uniformity, and contained dsRNA below the detection limit of the dot-blot assay. Spike protein expression was demonstrated, supporting the proposed production workflow as an effective strategy for generating structurally defined Cap2 mRNA.

title: Dual-Handle Purification for Structurally Defined Cap2 mRNA Using Hydrophobic Tag-Assisted Cap Chromatography and Oligo(dT) Affinity Chromatography.

abstract: The global COVID-19 health crisis threw into sharp focus the essential need for rapid, agile production of mRNA vaccines. Decreased processing time and reduction in equipment scale and footprint of continuous manufacture make its application to mRNA production highly attractive. Described here is one of the first demonstrations of integrated, continuous purification and concentration of mRNA vaccines via multicolumn Oligo dT (OdT) monolithic separation and subsequent single-pass tangential flow filtration (SPTFF). This simple, two-step continuous mRNA purification process presents a further streamlined schema relative to traditional batch operation thanks to a novel OdT elution strategy which obviates the need for final buffer exchange via diafiltration. Purification of mRNA in vitro transcription (IVT) product of two distinct constructs of variable length by the developed continuous multicolumn chromatography (MCC) capture methods successfully demonstrated comparable yield and purity to counterpart batch processes. Hollow fiber SPTFF also efficiently concentrated both mRNA constructs at relevant downstream volumetric throughputs with stable permeate flux profile while preserving step yields compared to batch TFF. Successful integration of these unit operations in flow was proved with purification of 175 mL of IVT product (75 mg mRNA) over the span of 16 OdT load events with yield > 97% and steady-state concentration factor of 12.2X. This work focuses on closing the gap in continuous purification of IVT product to generate drug substance (DS) toward the realization of a fully continuous mRNA manufacturing platform. Such a platform process would poise industry to quickly respond to rapid increases for vaccine demand.

title: A Platform Approach to Continuous mRNA Purification.

abstract: Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), which includes T cell receptor (TCR), chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), and tumor infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy, has emerged as a promising form of immunotherapy for the treatment of cancer, with multiple FDA approvals across the three classes. However, each class faces its own specific hurdles for the treatment of solid tumors. Here, we investigated whether intratumoral administration of mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encoding immune-stimulatory proteins would be a strategy to boost the efficacy of ACT for the treatment of solid tumors. As proof-of-concept to demonstrate the validity of this LNP strategy, we designed and validated mRNAs encoding a novel membrane-bound single-chain human IL-12 (mbIL-12) to reprogram the suppressive tumor microenvironment, as well as an anti-human mesothelin-CD3ε bispecific T cell engager (MSLN-TE) with the potential to address antigenic heterogeneity. We investigated intratumoral administration of mbIL-12 and MSLN-TE mRNA LNPs in the setting of the clinical stage NY-ESO-1 8F TCR, observing robust improvements in TCR T cell therapy efficacy upon intratumoral LNP administration in a murine xenograft model of human lung adenocarcinoma. While delivery of each mRNA construct individually improved TCR T cell therapy efficacy, combined delivery of both constructs resulted in an additive improvement in efficacy. This work sets the stage for the application of mRNA LNP technology to improve the efficacy of ACTs.

title: Localized lipid nanoparticle delivery of membrane bound IL-12 and T cell engager mRNA potentiates adoptive cell therapy in solid tumors.

abstract:
This is a multicenter, open-label, non-randomized, dose escalation, first-in-human (FIH) trial to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of CH505M5 N197D mRNA-gp160 and CH505 TF mRNA-gp160. Both products are mRNA encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) (subsequently referred to as mRNA-LNPs). The primary hypotheses are:

1. the CH505M5 N197D mRNA-gp160 will expand CH235-like B cell precursors,
2. the CH505 TF mRNA-gp160 will boost CH235-like bnAb B cell precursors to acquire more functional mutations needed for broadly neutralizing antibody (bnAb) development, and
3. these mRNA-LNPs will be safe and well tolerated among individuals living without HIV.

abstract: Theranostic nanomedicines are engineered multifunctional systems that integrate diagnostic sensing, imaging, and therapeutic delivery within a single nanoscale platform. Their performance depends not only on material composition but also on controllable nano-bio interactions, transport, targeting, stimulus responsiveness, and manufacturability. This review examines the bioengineering principles underlying next-generation theranostic nanomedicines, including lipid, polymeric, mesoporous silica, inorganic, extracellular-vesicle-derived, and cell-membrane-camouflaged platforms. Particular emphasis is placed on how physicochemical design governs protein-corona formation, circulation, biodistribution, cellular uptake, and clearance, and how endogenous or externally applied stimuli can be engineered for spatiotemporally controlled cargo release and imaging feedback. We further discuss the integration of multimodal imaging with nucleic-acid delivery, CRISPR/Cas gene editing, immunotherapy, ferroptosis, sonodynamic therapy, and photothermal therapy, together with emerging uses of artificial intelligence and machine learning for formulation optimization, image analysis, toxicity prediction, and treatment-response modeling. Despite rapid technological progress, clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous biological behavior, limited targeting efficiency, long-term safety uncertainties, complex manufacturing, batch-to-batch variability, and regulatory challenges. Future development should shift from increasingly complex multifunctional constructs toward platforms with measurable design-function relationships, scalable Good Manufacturing Practice-compatible production, standardized characterization, and clinically relevant validation. Such an engineering-focused approach could help advance theranostic nanomedicine from predominantly preclinical multifunctional systems toward reproducible technologies for precision diagnosis and therapy.

title: Engineering Theranostic Nanomedicines for Clinical Translation: Nano-Bio Interactions, Responsive Design, Multimodal Function, and Scale-Up.

abstract: Accurate and dynamic visualization of nucleic acids at the single-molecule level is essential for elucidating cellular processes, defining disease-associated molecular mechanisms, and advancing molecular diagnostics. Conventional imaging methods often lack the sensitivity, specificity, or spatiotemporal resolution required in complex biological systems. Engineered clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) technologies, leveraging the high programmability of Cas proteins and guide RNAs, have expanded nucleic acid imaging from repetitive and non-repetitive genomic loci to sequence-variant discrimination and individual RNA imaging. This review summarizes major engineering strategies, including Cas protein labeling, guide RNA scaffold modification, and nanomaterial- or protein-assisted signal amplification platforms. We further discuss biomedical applications in live-cell tracking, spatial nucleic acid analysis, and real-time monitoring of cellular dynamics. By examining the biochemical and engineering principles underlying these platforms, we provide a framework for the rational design of CRISPR-based nucleic acid imaging strategies and identify key considerations for overcoming persistent limitations in complex biological environments. Collectively, these advances position engineered CRISPR imaging as a programmable platform for spatially resolved nucleic acid analysis; however, broader application to clinically relevant specimens will require rigorous validation of quantitative robustness and specimen compatibility, together with standardized imaging workflows.

abstract: Staphylococcal bacteriophages with proven therapeutic efficacy in anti-staphylococcal therapy have large (~140 kb) genomes and belong to subfamily Twortvirinae. Representatives of four genera (Kayvirus, Silviavirus, Sepunavirus, and Twortvirus) are the most intensively studied and are advancing toward clinical applications. However, the functions of many of their genes remain unknown and cannot be predicted from sequence homology alone. The least explored and most diverse genomic regions are the long terminal repeats (LTRs), which comprise ~10% of the virion DNA. These regions were often omitted from early genome assemblies or misplaced in genomic maps. Only recent studies have shown that LTRs encode genes expressed immediately upon infection and involved in host takeover, genome establishment, and interactions with bacterial defense systems, highlighting their critical role in successful infection during phage therapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genomic architecture, transcriptional organization, and molecular functions of LTR regions in Twortvirinae phages. By integrating comparative genomics with recent transcriptomic and phage-host interaction studies, we identify LTRs as key regulatory and evolutionary hubs in Twortvirinae biology and highlight major knowledge gaps concerning their roles in bacterial immunity and phage genome evolution. The enrichment of LTRs in targets of bacterial anti-phage defense systems, together with their dynamic evolution through gene gain, loss, and diversification, suggests a central role in phage adaptation to diverse hosts. Finally, our synthesis of available data allows us, for the first time, to infer which end of the phage genome enters the host cell first during infection.

abstract: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a group of severe neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by early-onset seizures, developmental delay or regression, and cognitive impairment. Many DEEs arise from genetic variants that disrupt neuronal excitability, synaptic function, metabolism, cell signaling, or epigenetic regulation. As the genetic architecture of DEEs has expanded, genetic therapy has emerged as a promising strategy to address their underlying molecular causes. Preclinical studies using adeno-associated viral vectors, antisense oligonucleotides, RNA-based therapies, and CRISPR-derived approaches have shown that early intervention can reduce seizure burden, improve neurological phenotypes, and extend survival in selected models. These advances also highlight the importance of therapeutic timing, cell-type specificity, and appropriate vector design. In this Review, we adopt a mechanism-centered framework that links major biological classes of DEEs to gene therapy design parameters, including modality, vector, promoter, and developmental timing, while also considering translational challenges and future directions for precision medicine in this field.

abstract: Engineered cyanobacteria are promising microbial chassis for recombinant protein production and oral delivery, but low intracellular accumulation, expression-associated physiological burden, and residual antibiotic-resistance markers limit their application. Here, we developed an integrated protein-production and marker-removal strategy in Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and evaluated chromosomal reporter expression in Arthrospira platensis NIES-39. The CpcB-based expression configuration at the native phycocyanin locus resulted in markedly higher mVenus accumulation than free expression at the NSC1 neutral site, accompanied by reduced culture growth and altered photosynthetic characteristics. Incorporation of a tobacco etch virus protease recognition site, together with chromosomal TEV protease expression, enabled partial intracellular cleavage of the fusion protein. Sequential CRISPR-Cpf1 editing and SacB counterselection enabled the removal of targeted antibiotic-resistance cassettes in Synechocystis, as supported by locus-specific PCR and Sanger sequencing. Chromosomal mVenus expression was also established in A. platensis, although the complete marker-removal strategy was not successfully transferred to this host. Under zebrafish-oriented in vitro intestinal conditions, engineered Synechocystis exhibited pronounced structural disruption, whereas A. platensis filaments fragmented more gradually, accompanied by the release of intracellular components. Following zebrafish feeding, reporter-associated fluorescence was detected in the examined intestinal sections at 6 h after administration. Together, these results establish a Synechocystis engineering framework integrating enhanced recombinant protein accumulation, protease-mediated intracellular processing, and targeted antibiotic-marker removal, with complementary assessment of intestinal mVenus-associated fluorescence following oral administration.

abstract:
OBJECTIVE: rare interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) represent a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by various pathogenic mechanisms, clinical presentations, prognoses, and therapeutic challenges. Among these, acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD), pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH) exemplify rare pulmonary diseases driven by distinct biological mechanisms, including lysosomal dysfunction, impaired surfactant homeostasis, and activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) pathways. Recent advancements in molecular biology, genomics, and translational research boosted the development of precision medicine strategies and disease-specific therapies for these conditions.
STUDY DESIGN: this narrative review was conducted in accordance with the SANRA guidelines. A thorough literature search of the PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus databases was performed from January 2000 to June 2026.
RESULTS: significant progress has been made in treating all three diseases. In ASMD, enzyme replacement therapy with olipudase alfa has greatly improved visceral and lung symptoms, while research in gene therapy, gene editing, and metabolic treatments is ongoing. For PAP, inhaled granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) is now the primary disease-specific treatment, now supported by phase III trial evidence for inhaled molgramostim, complemented by potential therapies such as immunomodulation, macrophage transplantation, and gene-based strategies. In PLCH, the discovery of recurrent MAPK pathway variants has supported the use of genotype-targeted treatments with BRAF and MEK inhibitors. Under these conditions, advances in molecular diagnostics, circulating biomarkers, quantitative HRCT, radiomics, and artificial intelligence (AI) are poised to enhance diagnosis, patient stratification, prognosis, and treatment decisions.
CONCLUSIONS: ASMD, PAP and PLCH are entering into an era of precision medicine, in which disease-specific molecular mechanisms play an increasing role in guiding diagnosis and treatment. Ongoing integration of genomics, biomarkers, advanced imaging, AI, and targeted therapies could revolutionise the management of conditions such as ASMD, PAP, and PLCH, leading to better long-term patient outcomes.

title: The Therapeutic Pipeline: Future Treatments and Precision Medicine.

abstract: Accurate prediction of CRISPR/Cas9 off-target cleavage activity requires molecular representations that explicitly capture the interaction compatibility between guide RNA and target DNA. This study presents PriMPT, a prior-informed multiscale paired-token representation learning framework that redesigns guide-target tokenization using 1-, 2-, and 3-gram paired tokens and injects mechanism-informed pair-prior descriptors into the corresponding embeddings through scale-specific gated injection, thereby incorporating RNA-DNA interaction information before contextual modeling and facilitating interaction-aware learning of guide-target compatibility. Across guide-disjoint cross-validation on six public data sets and a cross-data set external test, PriMPT achieved the numerically highest mean area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) among the evaluated models in each of the seven scenarios, with ablation studies identifying input-level pair-prior injection as the most consistent contributor and Integrated Gradients analysis yielding attribution patterns consistent with established aspects of Cas9 target recognition. These results suggest that PriMPT captures mechanism-relevant sequence-pair patterns and offers a mechanism-informed representation learning strategy for CRISPR/Cas9 off-target risk assessment.

abstract: The purpose of this study is to test the safety and tolerability of BMN 351 in participants with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) with a genetic mutation amenable to exon 51 skipping.
description:
This is Phase 1/2, open-label, multi-center study consisting of 2 parts to evaluate the safety and tolerability of BMN 351 at escalating doses in participants with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) with genetic mutations amenable to exon 51 skipping.

Participants will be assigned to one of three groups called cohorts (Cohort 1, 2 or 3). Cohort 1 participants are further divided into Cohort 1A and Cohort 1B. In Cohort 1A, 3 participants will receive increasing doses once every 2 weeks with a visit to assess safety measures collected the week after dosing prior to escalating doses of BMN 351. In part 2, the participants in cohort 1A will transition to once weekly dosing. The participants in Cohort 1B, 2, and 3 will initiate low, medium, and high doses of BMN 351 and continue once weekly dosing at that same dose. The study will enroll approximately 18 participants.

abstract:
This Phase 2, multi-center, single-arm study evaluates the safety, tolerability, and activity of neoadjuvant PRTX007 in combination with pembrolizumab in participants with resectable Stage III melanoma. Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has demonstrated improved clinical outcomes compared with adjuvant-only approaches, but there remains a need to enhance pathologic response rates without significant added toxicity.

Participants will receive oral PRTX007, a Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) agonist prodrug, administered in combination with intravenous pembrolizumab prior to surgical resection. The primary objective is to determine the major pathologic response (MPR) rate following neoadjuvant therapy. Secondary objectives include evaluation of safety, pathologic complete response, event-free survival, overall survival, pharmacokinetics, and immune-related biomarkers.

This study aims to determine whether the addition of PRTX007 to pembrolizumab improves antitumor immune responses and clinical outcomes in patients with Stage III melanoma.

description:
This study investigates whether combining the TLR7 agonist PRTX007 with pembrolizumab enhances immune-mediated tumor response in the neoadjuvant setting for Stage III melanoma, with the goal of improving pathologic response rates and clinical outcomes while maintaining an acceptable safety profile.

Design This is a Phase 2, multi-center, open-label, single-arm study conducted in Australia. The study will enroll approximately 48 participants with resectable Stage III melanoma.

The study consists of two parts:

* Part A: 24 participants will be enrolled, including an initial dose-escalation safety run-in using a 3+3 design to evaluate tolerability and dose-limiting toxicities.
* Part B: An additional 24 participants will be enrolled if sufficient activity is observed in Part A.

Treatment Plan

Participants will receive neoadjuvant therapy consisting of:

* PRTX007: Oral administration for 3 days on and 4 days off per week for 9 cycles (7-day cycles)
* Pembrolizumab: 200 mg intravenous infusion every 3 weeks for 3 cycles Following completion of neoadjuvant therapy, participants will undergo definitive surgical resection.

Post-surgical treatment will be response-adapted:

* Participants achieving MPR may receive observation or pembrolizumab alone
* Participants without MPR will receive adjuvant PRTX007 in combination with pembrolizumab

abstract: The goal of this phase I trial is to evaluate the toxicity and feasibility of a tumor-specific RNA-NP vaccine in patients with stage IIB-IV melanoma who have evidence of progressive disease by RECIST 1.1 criteria while receiving adjuvant aPD1 therapy, or those who progress within 6 months of completion of adjuvant treatment, or unresectable stage II soft tissue sarcoma or stage III-IV soft tissue sarcoma.
description:
Melanoma is an increasing public health concern in the state of Florida. The advent of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) has revolutionized the treatment of advanced melanoma. Unfortunately, in the adjuvant setting, up to 30% of subjects will have disease recurrence within 1 year of starting ICI therapy. Previous studies have shown that subjects who progress while on adjuvant ICI treatment, or soon after completion, have a more aggressive course of disease that responds poorly to subsequent immunotherapy. One reason for the failure of ICI in the post adjuvant setting is the immune suppressive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME) and lack of professional APC activation. These APCs remain in an inert state unable to present tumor antigens for immune detection due to lack of innate immune activation and inhibition from myeloid derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Similarly, outside of rare subtypes, soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are enriched with an immunosuppressive TME leading to resistance to ICI therapy.

We have developed a novel RNA-lipid particle (RNA-LP) vaccine that simultaneously penetrates and reprograms the TME while inducing a tumor specific adaptive T cell response. This vaccine utilizes novel engineering design that layers tumor derived mRNA into a lipid-nanoparticle "onion-like" package along with pp65 full length lysosomal associated membrane protein (LAMP1) mRNA. These RNA-LPs localize to the TME and activate multiple innate pathways thereby activating APCs and suppressing the function of MDSCs. LAMP mRNA is added to improve innate activation as seen in preclinical modeling and to allow for tracking of T cell receptor specific immune response to vaccination. In this study we propose the use of subject derived RNA-LP vaccine in subjects who progress on, or soon after completion of adjuvant ICI. We propose that through re-priming of the antitumor immune response and alteration of the TME we can improve the efficacy of ICI therapy.

If effective, this treatment will revolutionize the management of this aggressive subset of melanoma and STS to improve overall survival. This study will also gather important information into the mechanisms of early ICI resistance, identify novel biomarkers of innate cell resistance and response to treatment, and provides a cutting edge, personalized immunology approach to treatment.

description:
This study will evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of 3 experimental HIV vaccines in adult participants without HIV and in overall good health in South Africa. The study vaccines are called mRNA-1645-eODGT8, mRNA-1645-CoreG28v2 and mRNA-1645-N332GT5.

The study will be conducted in two parts (Part A and B). Part A will include two Cohorts, each with 2 groups: Cohort 1A Group 1, Cohort 1A Group 2, Cohort 2A Group 3, and Cohort 2A Group 4. Part B will include two Cohorts, each with 2 groups: Cohort 1B Group 5, Cohort 1B Group 6, Cohort 2B Group 7, and Cohort 2B Group 8.

Participants in Part A Cohort 1A will be randomly assigned to receive mRNA-1645-eODGT8 followed by mRNA-1645-CoreG28v2 or to receive placebo. Participants in Part A Cohort 2A will be randomly assigned to receive two doses of the mRNA-1645-N332GT5 vaccine or to receive placebo. Cohorts 1A and 2A in Part A will be enrolled concurrently, and randomization to study product or placebo will take place in each cohort. Depending on their group, participants will receive 10 mcg of mRNA-1645-eODGT8, mRNA-1645-N332GT5 or Placebo by injection at Week 0 and 10 mcg of mRNA-1645-CoreG28v2, mRNA-1645-N332GT5, or Placebo at Week 8.

Participants in Part B Cohort 1B will be randomly assigned to receive an increased dose of the mRNA-1645-eODGT8 and mRNA-1645-CoreG28v2 vaccine or to receive placebo. Participants in Part B Cohort 2B will be randomly assigned to receive an increased dose of the mRNA-1645-N332GT5 vaccine or to receive placebo. Cohorts 1B and 2B in Part B will be enrolled concurrently, and randomization to study product or placebo will take place in each cohort. Depending on their group, participants will receive 30 mcg of mRNA-1645-eODGT8, mRNA-1645-N332GT5 or Placebo by injection at Week 0 and 30 mcg of mRNA-1645-CoreG28v2, mRNA-1645-N332GT5, or Placebo at Week 8.

Additional study visits will occur at Weeks 2, 7.5, 10, 15.5, and 24. Study visits may include physical examinations, medical history, vaccine injections, blood and urine collection, electrocardiogram, leukapheresis, lymph node cell collection, pregnancy test, HIV testing, risk reduction counseling, and questionnaires.

abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder for which no disease-modifying therapy currently exists. Gene therapy using adeno-associated virus (AAV) has become a potential experimental intervention for the molecular etiology of mutant huntingtin (mHTT). This review is a critical analysis of the present state of AAV-based therapeutic interventions that may be considered through the lens of translational preparedness instead of early clinical efficacy. Relevant literature was searched in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for studies published from January 2020 to June 2026, using keywords related to Huntington's disease, AAV gene therapy, gene silencing, genome editing, safety, and clinical translation. The essential factors are the design of vectors, delivery methods, the mechanistic differences between gene silencing and editing, and safety issues raised due to preliminary clinical trials. The issues of ethical, regulatory, and health-system preparedness, which include neurosurgical risks, patient selection, long-term monitoring, and regulatory divergence between the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), European Medicines Agency (EMA) and Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), are assessed in terms of their influence on clinical scalability. We emphasize on the unbridgeable disconnect between the experimental promise and the true applicability by combining trial evidence with regulatory and implementation understanding. Long-term sustainability of AAV therapies will depend on decade-long safety surveillance, transparent governance, and coordinated health-system readiness.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) can enable efficient delivery of mRNA for gene editing, making LNPs a promising vector for therapeutic treatment of inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs). Currently, LNP targeting of photoreceptors is inefficient and inconsistent between different cargos. We aimed to mimic the photoreceptor tropism of viral vectors by attaching adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid surface peptide derivatives to LNPs. We identified the most promising AAV capsid-derived peptides for photoreceptor uptake by confocal microscopy of retinal cross-sections. We generated LNP variants by surface conjugation of top performing peptides to maleimide-polyethylene glycol (PEG)-lipids. Peptide-conjugated LNPs delivered mRNA to photoreceptors and retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) in mice, with GS4, a peptide derived from the AAV9 capsid, as the top performer. Subretinal delivery of 1.0% peptide conjugated GS4-LNPs encapsulating Cre mRNA shows an 8.7-fold increase in photoreceptor transfection in the treated area compared to standard LNPs, respectively. However, when GS4-LNPs encapsulated Cas9 mRNA and sgAi9 editing was restricted to the RPE, reaching 10.9% editing of the total RPE and 31.3% editing within the treated area. Our novel GS4-LNP formulation demonstrates the feasibility for AAV peptide conjugation to LNPs and illuminates the bottlenecks in LNP-mRNA delivery to photoreceptors across mRNA payloads.

title: AAV peptide-conjugated LNPs highlight bottlenecks in LNP-mRNA delivery to photoreceptors.

abstract: This study explores the therapeutic potential of the calcium-activated potassium channel KCa3.1 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Increased KCa3.1 expression correlates with poor overall survival of patients with PDAC. Using the immunocompetent KPfC (KrasWT/LSL-G12D Tp53fl/+ Pdx1-Cre) mouse model, we evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of KCa3.1 inhibition with TRAM-34 and maurotoxin alone or in combination with gemcitabine. Mechanistic insights were obtained in vitro from KCa3.1 CRISPR knockout pancreatic cancer cells (PANC-1KCNN4-/-) and a three-dimensional mixed spheroid model composed of pancreatic cancer and stellate cells. In vivo, KCa3.1 inhibition combined with gemcitabine decreased growth of tumor nodes and counteracted gemcitabine-induced fibrosis. Consistently, in vitro and ex vivo data showed that KCa3.1 inhibition induced tumor cell death and altered the invasive phenotype. Here, maurotoxin outperformed TRAM-34. On a molecular level, KCa3.1 inhibition diminished epithelial-mesenchymal transition, reduced T cell exhaustion markers and TGF-β1 secretion, and downregulated the G2-M checkpoint. These findings can mechanistically account for the therapeutic benefits of targeting KCa3.1 channels in PDAC.

title: Targeting KCa3.1 channels in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma impairs disease progression.

abstract: The ability to modulate the tumor microenvironment emerges as a compelling strategy to stimulate antitumor immunity in solid tumors. In this context, innate immune cells, especially macrophages, are interesting targets for immunotherapies. Approaches based on CRISPR to delete specific suppressive molecules in these cells might lead to antitumor immunity. The target molecules to be depleted will depend on the type of tumor, since the tumor microenvironment and its immune-suppressive regulators can vary. This correspondence aims to discuss published animal models and stimulate research in this critical subject for the improvement of immunotherapies targeting macrophages. New therapeutic strategies, including epigenetic modifications to stabilize the proinflammatory phenotypes of these cells, are underscored.

title: Macrophages as targets for adoptive cell therapy against solid tumors.

abstract: The accelerating aging of the global population has made aging and its related diseases major public health challenges in the 21st century. Adipose tissue is not only an energy reservoir but also a crucial endocrine organ and metabolic regulator. Its dysfunction is closely linked to aging and the development of multiple diseases. This review outlines the key characteristics of adipocyte senescence and discusses its pathological contributions to obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases. It also summarizes current intervention strategies for adipocyte senescence, including senolytics, senomorphics, caloric restriction, physical exercise, and gene editing. We propose lipid prodrugs as promising adipose tissue delivery platforms that can be coupled with diverse therapeutic agents to increase the local concentration of drugs and minimize systemic toxicity. By utilizing the unique lipid metabolism of adipocytes, this strategy offers a new avenue for therapeutic intervention in adipocyte senescence and its associated metabolic disorders.

abstract: Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) is a highly conserved serine/threonine kinase that orchestrates key processes in mitotic progression, DNA damage repair, apoptosis, and immune signaling. Its frequent overexpression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) correlates with tumor aggressiveness, poor prognosis, and resistance to therapy, highlighting its significance as both a biomarker and therapeutic target. This review systematically evaluates the molecular mechanisms by which PLK1 drives NSCLC pathogenesis, including its regulation by transcription factors, tumor suppressors, oncogenes, non-coding RNAs, and signaling pathways. We highlight PLK1's role in promoting cell cycle progression, chromosomal instability, metastasis, immune escape, and therapeutic resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted agents. Furthermore, we summarize preclinical and clinical advances in PLK1-directed therapies, encompassing small-molecule inhibitors, RNA interference, gene editing, PROTACs, and nanomedicine-based strategies, with an emphasis on their potential to enhance sensitivity to existing treatments. Collectively, current evidence establishes PLK1 as a central hub in NSCLC biology and a promising candidate for precision oncology. Future investigations should prioritize biomarker-driven clinical trials, combinatorial strategies, and next-generation inhibitors for overcoming resistance and improving patient outcomes.

abstract: This issue of the Biomedical Journal explores therapeutic approaches to neuroinflammation, antimicrobial resistance, and cancer, as well as developments in laboratory testing and prognostic assessment. Experimental findings show that glibenclamide attenuates palmitic acid-induced hippocampal inflammation and memory impairment in mice. In antimicrobial research, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated elimination of resistance genes restores ertapenem susceptibility in resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates, while deep learning offers an approach to interpreting antimicrobial susceptibility tests from images. Oncology articles span molecular characterization, treatment, and prognosis: BK polyomavirus integration and aristolochic acid exposure are associated with distinct molecular features in kidney transplant-associated urothelial carcinomas; bavachinin enhances cisplatin's antitumor activity in oral cancer models; biomarker changes inform prognosis during radium-223 therapy; and external validation supports the MAGIC-D model in advanced biliary tract cancer. Furthermore, research on cartilage homeostasis examines exercise-dependent responses of Prg4-expressing cells. Correspondence addresses combined radiotherapy and systemic treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma and, in a second exchange, stewardship of short-term systemic corticosteroid use.

title: The weight of memory: nutrition, diabetes, and the brain.

abstract: Aberrant glycosylation reshapes tumour-host communication through glycan-protein interactions, driving immune evasion, invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. These interactions regulate signalling between tumour cells and their microenvironment, influencing disease progression and clinical outcomes. This review summarises the structural basis of glycan recognition and its functional roles in tumour progression, with emphasis on glycan-lectin interactions, immune modulation, extracellular matrix remodelling, and angiogenesis. We further discuss recent advances in glycan-based biomarkers, glycoproteomic profiling, glycomimetic therapeutics, glycan-targeted antibodies, and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence-assisted glycomics and CRISPR-based glycoengineering. Collectively, these advances highlight the translational potential of glycan-protein interactions for improving cancer diagnosis, patient stratification, and the development of precision therapies targeting tumour-associated glycosylation.

title: Glycan-Protein Interactions in Tumour Progression, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Targeting.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Telomerase activity is primarily controlled by expression of the catalytic subunit hTERT, yet the mechanisms coordinating its transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation remain incompletely understood. Paradoxically, hypermethylation of a CpG-rich region upstream of the hTERT transcription start site, termed the TERT Hypermethylated Oncological Region (THOR), is strongly associated with hTERT activation. Recent evidence suggests that THOR methylation influences the expression of hTAPAS, a long non-coding RNA transcribed antisense to the hTERT promoter that represses hTERT expression. Here, we investigated the relationship between DNA methylation and alternative splicing of hTERT.
RESULTS: Using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated targeted enrichment combined with Nanopore sequencing, we generated high-resolution DNA methylation maps across several kilobases surrounding the hTERT promoter and intronic regions encompassing exons 6-8 in multiple human cell lines. These analyses identified distinct methylation signatures associated with specific hTERT splice isoform profiles. Functional perturbation experiments further demonstrated that altering the epigenetic state of the hTERT locus influences alternative splicing. Overexpression of the antisense long non-coding RNA hTAPAS, as well as treatment with the DNA demethylating agent 5'-azacytidine, reduced CpG methylation at the hTERT promoter and altered the distribution of hTERT splice isoforms. These findings indicate an association among hTAPAS expression, DNA methylation at the hTERT locus, and hTERT splice isoform profiles.
CONCLUSIONS: Our results identify an association between DNA methylation patterns at the hTERT locus and alternative hTERT splicing and further implicate hTAPAS expression in this regulatory context. These results support an epigenetic mechanism linking hTAPAS to hTERT promoter methylation and splice isoform selection, providing new insight into how telomerase regulation may be remodeled during development and cancer.

abstract:
The purpose of this study is to learn about the safety and effects of an updated COVID-19 vaccine (called BNT162b2) in adults 18 to 64 years of age.

This study is seeking participants who:

* are medically stable
* have not had a recent COVID-19 infection
* have not had a recent vaccination
* do not have medical conditions that increase their risk of complications from COVID-19

All participants in this study will randomly receive 1 injection into their arm of either:

* BNT162b2 vaccine which targets COVID-19 and is selected for the 2026-2027 COVID-19 season, or
* Tdap vaccine which targets tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (whooping cough).

The study team and participants will not know which injection they receive. We will evaluate safety and may evaluate SARS-CoV-2 spike protein levels in people receiving each of these vaccines.

Participants will be in the study for about 2 months.

abstract: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is a heritable cardiac disorder commonly linked to alterations in desmosomal proteins. While desmosomal dysfunction is a recognized pathogenic mechanism, the early molecular remodeling that precedes clinical manifestations remains unclear. Here we used a mouse model with inducible cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of Pkp2 (encoding plakophilin-2) and performed time-resolved mass spectrometry-based proteomics to map disease progression from early PKP2 loss to structural remodeling. Molecular changes preceded phenotypic abnormalities, and spatial asymmetry was evident, with earlier and more pronounced proteome remodeling in the right ventricle despite comparable PKP2 depletion in both ventricles. Downregulation of protein networks spanning desmosomes, sarcomeres and mitochondria suggests their functional coupling, with mitochondrial remodeling emerging as an early and progressively worsening feature. Intervention with honokiol attenuated changes across the major protein networks, highlighting mitochondrial pathways as promising therapeutic targets and honokiol as a potential strategy to delay arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy progression. Our findings provide critical insights into the concealed stage of disease progression and identify molecular targets for early intervention.

abstract: Highly pathogenic Hendra and Nipah viruses encode accessory P gene products (C, V and W) that antagonize innate immunity and contribute to pathogenicity. Cedar virus (CedV), an apathogenic bat-borne henipavirus, is presumed to lack P gene mRNA editing and therefore is unable to express V and W proteins. Here, we identify CedV peptides originating from a frameshifted P gene open reading frame and demonstrate a previously unrecognized, noncanonical editing site at a homopolymeric adenine tract that introduces single-nucleotide A or G insertion. This mRNA editing produces a protein that we refer to as U protein, whose C-terminal domain shares sequence and predicted structural features with those of the henipavirus V protein. Recombinant CedV mutants defective in mRNA editing were only recoverable by trans-complementation and showed markedly reduced release of infectious virus in cell culture and attenuated replication in mice lacking type I interferon receptor. Our data revise the CedV gene expression models and reveal a noncanonical editing mechanism that supports the production of a U protein critical for efficient infectious virus release. These results expand the fundamental concepts of paramyxovirus gene expression and reveal an unexpected requirement for P-gene editing in efficient infectious-virus production, with implications for the evaluation of potentially high-consequence paramyxoviruses.

abstract: BackgroundNusinersen treatment of adults with 5q-SMA was found to be safe and stabilizes or improves motor function in the short-term (<38 months), but data examining longer-term (>38 months) impact and safety is lacking.ObjectiveTo study the long-term (24-60 months) effects and safety profile of nusinersen in adults with 5q-SMA.MethodsWe conducted a observational study of 5q-SMA patients, age ≥18 years, and receiving nusinersen for ≥24 months. Data were analyzed by ambulatory status. Clinical outcomes included: 6-minute walk test (6MWT), Hammersmith Functional Motor Scale - Expanded (HFMSE) scores, revised upper limb module (RULM) scores, pulmonary function test results, and medication-related adverse effects. Data were collected at baseline and post-treatment initiation at months 2, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, and 60 +/- 2 months. Linear mixed models with random intercept for each patient were used to examine the changes of outcomes across time.ResultsThiry-two individuals with 5q-SMA (17 female) were included. Nineteen were non-ambulatory (mean age 38.3+/- 12.1 years) and 13 were ambulatory (mean age 32.9+/-9.5 years) at treatment onset. Average treatment duration was 53.3 months (range 24-60 months). The ambulatory group showed stability in 6MWT and HFMSE compared to baseline. In non-ambulatory patients, RULM and FVC remained stable. No serious adverse events attributable to nusinersen were reported.ConclusionsLong-term nusinersen treatment is safe in adults with SMA. Patients showed relative clinical stability over 60 months. These findings suggest that nusinersen may provide relative improvement compared to the natural disease progression over 2-5 years of treatment.

abstract: Human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), comprising embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), have emerged as a versatile platform connecting developmental biology with disease modelling, drug discovery, and regenerative medicine. Their capacity for indefinite self-renewal and differentiation into derivatives of all three germ layers provides an essentially renewable source of human cells that are otherwise inaccessible from patients. In this review, we discuss the biological principles governing hPSC identity, with emphasis on the transcriptional, epigenetic, metabolic, and extracellular signalling networks that regulate pluripotency and the distinct features of naive and primed states. We further examine culture systems for maintaining pluripotency and directed differentiation strategies for generating lineage-specific cell types. The application of hPSCs to disease modelling and therapeutic discovery is considered through two-dimensional cellular models and increasingly sophisticated three-dimensional organoids and organoid-on-chip systems, which provide progressively greater tissue complexity and physiological relevance. We also highlight the integration of CRISPR-based genome editing with hPSC platforms to generate isogenic disease models, establish genotype-phenotype relationships, identify therapeutic targets, and enable precise correction of disease-associated variants. Finally, we review the emerging clinical applications of hPSC-derived cell therapies and clinical translation, which remains constrained by challenges related to genomic stability, cellular heterogeneity and maturation, immune compatibility, tumorigenicity, manufacturing, and scalability. Addressing these challenges through improved differentiation, quality control, genome engineering, and scalable manufacturing will be essential for translating the broad potential of hPSCs into safe, reproducible, and accessible clinical therapies.

title: The translational journey of human pluripotent stem cells.

abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics have transformed modern medicine, enabling targeted treatments that address a wide range of diseases at their genetic roots. From RNAi-mediated gene silencing to mRNA vaccines and CRISPR-based editing, these advances offer precision strategies for previously intractable conditions. The success of these modalities hinges entirely on delivery technologies which have evolved lockstep with nucleic acid research, facilitating transport from administration site to intracellular target(s). Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the leading delivery platform for nucleic acid therapeutics which is partially due to extensive research and development of lipid-based vehicle derivatives previously developed for small molecule-based drugs. While LNPs themselves have a relatively brief clinical history, the COVID-19 pandemic propelled nucleic acid technologies into the global spotlight, accelerating public, industrial, and regulatory engagement. This surge in attention catalyzed the maturation of clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory frameworks for therapies that rely on delivery technologies like LNPs for success. While this progress has enabled a new wave of therapies, it has also underscored the limitations of LNPs, including poor penetration into dense extracellular matrix (ECM) tissues and dose-limiting toxicities driven by immunogenicity. As optimization of LNP formulations continues, a new generation of nanoparticle platforms is emerging, aiming to address these shortcomings in morphology, chemistry, and tissue specificity. These platforms are well-positioned to leverage the translational groundwork laid by LNPs, potentially accelerating their own path to clinical relevance. In this review, we examine the evolution and clinical impact of LNPs, analyze their key limitations, and explore emerging delivery platforms, such as biomimetic nanoparticles and polymeric systems that seek to overcome the physicochemical limitations of LNPs while building on the lessons and regulatory frameworks they established.

title: Lipid nanoparticles and their successors: Design principles for dense tissue penetration and clinical translation.

abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have transformed cancer therapy, yet resistance limits durable benefit. N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most prevalent internal mRNA modification, dynamically regulates RNA stability, translation, and noncoding RNA function via writers, erasers, and readers, shaping antigen presentation, checkpoint expression, interferon signaling, and immune-cell activation. Emerging evidence indicates that m6A-dependent immune resistance involves tumor-intrinsic programs and multicellular, metabolically conditioned niches. Hypoxia-associated m6A remodeling, lactate/glycolysis-driven suppression, lipid metabolic rewiring, extracellular vesicle-mediated RNA transfer, m6A-regulated circRNAs and lncRNAs, and stromal or spatial immune exclusion collectively promote CD8+ T-cell dysfunction, Treg and myeloid cell enrichment, macrophage polarization, impaired antigen presentation, and resistance predominantly to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade, with more limited direct evidence linking these programs to resistance to CTLA-4 blockade. Here, we synthesize current evidence linking m6A regulators and m6A-modified RNA networks to immune checkpoint therapy failure, emphasizing metabolic and RNA-mediated resistance niches. We also discuss candidate biomarker models integrating m6A regulator expression, target RNA signatures, metabolic features, and immune-context characteristics, as well as therapeutic strategies targeting m6A enzymes, reader proteins, ncRNA circuits, metabolic dependencies, and delivery-based interventions. Key translational challenges, including context-dependent effects, cell-type specificity, spatial heterogeneity, delivery limitations, off-target toxicity, and the need for clinical validation, are highlighted. Understanding m6A as an adaptive epitranscriptomic interface may refine biomarker-guided immunotherapy and rational combination strategies.

abstract: Although lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have been widely used for mRNA delivery, understanding how cholesterol analogues modulate LNP properties and intracellular trafficking to enhance transfection efficiency remains essential for the rational design of next-generation delivery systems. This study investigated their structure-activity relationships and effects on mRNA delivery. We hypothesized that C-24 alkyl-substituted phytosterols enhance transfection by modulating LNP physicochemical properties and interactions with intracellular transport proteins. These phytosterols altered LNP mechanics and morphology, promoting cellular uptake. In vitro results and molecular dynamics simulations revealed differential interactions between phytosterols and Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1), a late endosomal membrane protein involved in intracellular cholesterol transport. These interactions influenced the late-endosomal retention of phytosterol-substituted LNPs and contributed to enhanced transfection. Furthermore, rather than simply prolonging retention, phytosterol substitution modulated LNP trafficking kinetics, establishing a formulation-dependent optimal intracellular residence window. In vivo results demonstrated reduced serum levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in mice receiving phytosterol-substituted LNPs. Collectively, these findings elucidate how cholesterol analogues regulate LNP physicochemical properties and intracellular trafficking, providing mechanistic insights and design principles for developing more efficient and precise mRNA delivery systems.

title: Naturallyoccurring phytosterols in lipid nanoparticles induce rigidity reshape and endosome retention to enhance intracellular mRNA processing.

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding the chemical and formulation space explored for nucleic acid lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), but accurate assay prediction does not by itself establish useful delivery in vivo. This critical narrative review examines how evidence links molecular design, complete formulation identity, and biological context to cell-resolved function, with a focus on mRNA. We distinguish tissue accumulation from functional cargo delivery, membrane damage from productive release, and target-cell coverage from panel-restricted on-target precision. Four purposively selected cases illustrate distinct inference problems: AGILE's selected-candidate association and reformulation, Hamilton's non-AI accumulation screen and functional follow-up, LANTERN's benchmark using AGILE-derived data, and Wang's delivery-classification and pKa-regression workflow with changes between screening rounds. We propose a claim-specific evidence audit and a prospective comparison whose primary outcome is the number of confirmed qualifying formulations found within a declared resource ceiling. Manufacturing, storage, and tolerability are considered where they constrain the application. Neither the audit nor the comparison design has been empirically validated. They identify testable requirements for evaluating whether AI improves a declared delivery decision.

abstract: Ovarian cancer, particularly high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), remains a leading cause of gynecologic cancer mortality. Although HGSOC responds to platinum-taxane therapy, 70-85% relapse, with acquired resistance playing a major role. The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, centered on AKT, contributes to this resistance. Current literature examines AKT's downstream consequences in isolation, overlooking their collective contribution to tumor evolution; this review addresses that gap by separating upstream AKT activation from downstream resistance outputs. Intrinsic genomic alterations (PIK3CA mutation, phosphatase and tensin homolog [PTEN] loss) and extrinsic tumor microenvironment (TME) cues converge on AKT, which drives four emerging resistance mechanisms (metabolic reprogramming and ferroptosis evasion, epigenetic modulation of homologous recombination inhibitor sensitivity, cancer stem cell plasticity, and immune evasion, discussed with therapeutic targeting), integrated with classical mechanisms into a unified chemoresistance framework. AKT promotes chemoresistance by coordinating ATP-binding cassette transporter-mediated drug efflux, RAD51/BRCA-dependent DNA repair, and an elevated apoptotic threshold via Bcl-2-associated agonist of cell death and survivin modulation. Spatial organization and interconnections are highlighted, including amplified AKT activation at the tumor-stromal interface through cancer-associated fibroblast-derived exosomal PTEN silencing. We evaluate therapeutic strategies (AKT and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors, folate receptor alpha-targeted antibody-drug conjugates such as mirvetuximab soravtansine, and metabolic modulation through the AKT/mTORC1 axis) by targeting multiple nodes simultaneously. Patient-derived organoids, CRISPR/Cas9 screening, and circulating tumor DNA monitoring enable clinical translation, supporting rationally designed combinations over sequential monotherapy and reframing AKT from a poor-prognosis marker to a therapeutic target in recurrent, chemoresistant ovarian cancer.

abstract: Metabolic disorders are increasingly associated with intestinal dysfunction and colorectal diseases, yet the pathological characteristics and underlying mechanisms of intestinal injury under metabolic stress remain poorly understood. Here, we established a transgenic (TG) Bama pig model by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of three humanized susceptibility genes and subjected the pigs to a high-fat, high-sugar diet (HFHSD) for 4, 8, or 12 months to investigate metabolic disorder-associated colonic dysfunction. HFHSD intervention induced marked alterations in serum biochemical parameters and disrupted colonic mucosal architecture, characterized by glandular disorganization and crypt distortion. Colonic tissues from TG pigs exhibited reduced populations of goblet cells, CD8⁺ T cells, and CD79A⁺ B cells, accompanied by pronounced activation of mitophagy, indicating impaired epithelial barrier integrity and mucosal immune homeostasis. In parallel, microbial diversity and IgA levels were reduced in the colonic contents of TG pigs, accompanied by an increased abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria, particularly Escherichia-Shigella. Metabolomic profiling of colonic contents further revealed significant alterations in the intestinal metabolic landscape, including decreased levels of isobutyric acid and isovaleric acid and an increased level of myristic acid, a metabolite associated with autophagy-related processes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that metabolic disorders are associated with coordinated alterations in colonic mucosal integrity, mucosal immunity, mitochondrial quality control, gut microbiota, and intestinal metabolism. The humanized TG Bama pig model provides a clinically relevant large-animal platform for investigating the pathophysiology of metabolic disorder-associated colonic diseases and may facilitate the development and preclinical evaluation of therapeutic strategies targeting intestinal dysfunction.

abstract: Germline mutations in PARN cause dyskeratosis congenita (DC), an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by multilineage cytopenia and progression to myeloid disease. The mechanisms underlying this malignant transformation have not been fully elucidated. Here we show, using a loss-of-function CRISPR-Cas9 zebrafish parn mutant, hematopoietic stem and progenitor (HSPC) expansion and reduced mature hematopoietic cells across various lineages. Cholesterol biosynthesis was transcriptionally activated; a finding recapitulated in patient-derived iPSCs with PARN mutations. Inhibiting cholesterol biosynthesis rescued HSPC expansion and anemia in parn mutants. Concurrent myeloid differentiation therapy or Wnt inhibition reduced HSPCs to varying degrees. We further demonstrate a role for activated Erk signaling in impairing erythrocyte differentiation and show robust rescue with trametinib treatment. Overall, our findings uncover unrecognized roles for Parn in regulating cholesterol metabolism and Erk signaling and provide preclinical evidence for targeting these pathways to restore hematopoiesis in DC.

abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether common genetic variants at the chromosome 1p13 locus that predisposes to Paget's disease of bone (PDB) regulate macrophage colony stimulating factor (M-CSF) expression in bone cells and to determine whether there is dysregulation of M-CSF in patients with PDB.
METHODS: The regions surrounding single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) previously associated with PDB at a genome wide significant level were deleted in clones of MG63 osteoblast-like cells using CRISPR/Cas, and levels of M-CSF mRNA and protein were evaluated in cells with and without deletions. Serum M-CSF was measured by ELISA in PDB and controls, and values in patients were related to clinical features of PDB and biochemical markers of bone remodelling.
RESULTS: Deletion of the region surrounding rs484959 increased expression of M-CSF mRNA by 1.31-fold (95% CI: 1.04, 1.58; P = 0.026) and M-CSF protein by 1.91-fold (95% CI: 1.25, 2.57; P = 0.013), compared with control cells. Serum M-CSF was significantly elevated in PDB vs controls (mean [S.D.] 781.7 [678] vs 541 [491] pg/ml, P < 0.001). Furthermore, M-CSF levels were associated with number of affected bones (P = 0.029), bodily pain assessed by SF-36 (P = 0.026) and biochemical markers of bone turnover.
CONCLUSION: The rs484959 SNP is a regulatory variant that modulates M-CSF mRNA and protein expression in osteoblasts. Serum M-CSF is increased in PDB and is associated with pain, disease extent and biochemical markers of bone remodelling. This suggests that there is dysregulation of M-CSF in PDB and that this cytokine may play a role in pathogenesis of the disease.

abstract: Interferons (IFNs) are cytokines critical for natural killer (NK) cell development, activation, cytotoxicity, and anti-tumor function. In this review, we examine how type I and type II IFNs shape NK cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity, with an emphasis on recent advances and their implications for NK cell-based cancer therapy. Although IFNs have traditionally been viewed as immune activating cytokines and biomarkers of effective anti-tumor immunity, emerging evidence suggests that their effects in cancer are highly context dependent. By integrating recent CRISPR screening studies in NK cells, mechanistic analyses of IFN signaling in NK cell therapy, and emerging evidence on IFN-NK cell crosstalk within the tumor microenvironment, we highlight a central paradox: while IFNs can enhance NK cell activation and tumor surveillance, they can also drive dysfunction, tumor immune adaptation, and therapeutic resistance under chronic or dysregulated conditions. This distinction is particularly important in solid tumors, where NK cell therapies continue to face major barriers, including poor tumor infiltration, limited persistence, and suppression by the tumor microenvironment. We propose that IFN signaling may be one underappreciated factor contributing to the highly variable efficacy of NK cell therapy across cancer models. Therefore, IFNs should not be understood simply as pro-inflammatory or anti-tumor signals. Instead, they function as dynamic immune regulators whose effects depend on timing, dose, duration, cellular source, and tumor context. We further discuss the current clinical landscape of IFN-NK therapies, including IFN-α and INF-β drugs, CAR-NK cell therapy, STING agonists, and other rational combination strategies. Future research should develop physiologically relevant and tumor-microenvironment representative model systems to investigate the effects of IFN signaling on NK cell anti-tumor function across distinct tumor types. Coordinated investigation of NK, cytokine, and tumor biology will accelerate clinically actionable strategies that leverage the NK-IFN axis.

title: The Role of Interferons in Regulating and Mediating NK Cell Anti-Tumor Immunity.

abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory bowel disease characterised by continuous inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa, resulting from complex interactions among genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and dysregulated immune responses. Although conventional therapies, including aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, biologics, and small-molecule drugs have improved disease control, their clinical utility remains limited by incomplete therapeutic responses, adverse effects, loss of efficacy, and difficulties in achieving sustained remission. The present review offers an in-depth view of the emerging trends in molecular pharmacology and future drug-delivery systems for UC. UC-relevant molecular targets and pathological features of the colonic microenvironment be matched to site-specific or stimulus-responsive delivery strategies to improve local therapeutic exposure while limiting systemic toxicity, and clinical translation have been described. We discuss recent therapeutic advances targeting key inflammatory pathways (e.g. TNF-α, JAK-STAT, TYK2, IL-23/Th17, S1P receptors and PPAR-γ) and microbiome-directed approaches (e.g. faecal microbiota transplantation, microbial metabolites and postbiotics). Biomarker-driven approaches, such as faecal calprotectin and microbiota profiling, are emphasised as key components of precision medicine and treatment monitoring. Advanced Drug delivery mechanisms such as liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, solid lipid nanoparticles, hydrogels, microparticles, nanogels and multifunctional theranostic systems provide opportunities for colon-specific drug delivery, controlled release, improved bioavailability, improved mucosal targeting and decreased systemic exposure. New approaches based on RNA-based therapeutics, CRISPR/Cas technologies and artificial intelligence-assisted drug delivery system design further increase the possibilities of personalised treatment. To summarise, the combination of molecularly targeted pharmacology with intelligent and site-specific drug-delivery technologies is an exciting avenue for enhancing therapeutic efficacy and reducing treatment-related toxicity and for furthering personalised management of UC. However, translation to widespread clinical practice will need to overcome challenges related to biocompatibility, gastrointestinal variability, scalability, manufacturing, controlled release, and regulatory approval.

title: Precision drug delivery for ulcerative colitis: engineering the colonic microenvironment for site-specific and responsive therapy.

abstract: Localized CRISPR-mediated CD47 ablation represents a potential alternative to systemic antibody-based therapy, with the possibility of reducing systemic toxicity associated with CD47 targeting. However, clinical translation is constrained by the limited cargo capacity of AAV vectors, which precludes packaging conventional Cas9/Cas12a systems into a single AAV vector. Here, we evaluated and optimized existing hypercompact CRISPR-Cas12f systems for efficient CD47 disruption and localized single-AAV delivery. Through systematic benchmarking, we identified AsCas12f-HKRA as a suitable editor for mouse Cd47 editing, achieving >60% editing efficiency comparable to enAsCas12a-HF while maintaining a favorable specificity profile. CD47 ablation enhanced macrophage phagocytosis in vitro and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. We then developed SOLO-CD47 (Single-AAV Optimized for Localized On-target-editing of CD47), an all-in-one AAV strategy incorporating a tandem dual-sgRNA expression cassette to overcome limited sgRNA expression from a single cassette. Intratumoral delivery of SOLO-CD47 suppressed tumor growth without detectable short-term hematologic abnormalities, and immune profiling revealed increased frequencies of F4/80+ CD86+ macrophage-associated cells and CD8+ T cells in SOLO-mCD47-treated tumors. The human-targeting strategy of SOLO-CD47 also achieved >60% CD47 editing across multiple human cancer cell lines. Collectively, these findings provide proof-of-concept for localized CRISPR-Cas12f-mediated CD47 editing using a single-AAV strategy in cancer immunotherapy.
