title: SOLO-CD47: an all-in-one AAV strategy for localized CRISPR-Cas12f-mediated CD47 editing in cancer immunotherapy.

abstract: Precision gene targeting has emerged as a powerful approach for selectively regulating gene expression and modifying disease-associated genetic pathways. Among the principal technologies, small interfering RNA (siRNA), microRNA (miRNA), CRISPR-Cas9, and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) provide distinct yet complementary strategies for gene regulation and genome manipulation. siRNAs mediate sequence-specific post-transcriptional gene silencing through degradation of complementary messenger RNA, enabling potent and generally transient suppression of target genes. In contrast, miRNAs are endogenous regulatory RNAs that modulate multiple transcripts through translational repression and mRNA destabilization, thereby influencing diverse cellular processes and regulatory networks. CRISPR-Cas9 expands the scope of precision gene targeting by enabling programmable modification of genomic DNA, whereas CRISPRi uses catalytically inactive Cas9 to achieve targeted transcriptional repression without introducing DNA double-strand breaks. This review provides a comparative and critical analysis of these technologies, emphasizing their molecular mechanisms, target recognition, specificity, delivery strategies, therapeutic applications, clinical development, advantages, limitations, and safety considerations. Collectively, these platforms have demonstrated therapeutic potential across a broad range of diseases, including cancer, genetic and metabolic disorders, cardiovascular and neurological diseases, infectious diseases, and ocular disorders. However, important barriers to clinical translation remain, including delivery limitations, molecular stability, target and off-target effects, immunogenicity, toxicity, genomic instability, and the need for precise and durable control of gene modulation. For CRISPR-based approaches, additional considerations include modality-specific genomic alterations, prolonged editor activity, and the ethical and regulatory implications of permanent genome modification. Continued advances in molecular engineering, delivery technologies, target-selection strategies, and platform optimization may improve the specificity, safety, durability, and therapeutic efficacy of these approaches and facilitate their responsible integration into precision medicine.

title: Precision gene targeting: comparative roles of siRNA, miRNA, and CRISPR technologies in gene silencing and genome editing: a review.

abstract: Targeted gene editing enables controlled integration and consistent expression of a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) in natural killer (NK) cells. We present a protocol for homology-directed repair-mediated CAR knockin into the AAVS1 safe-harbor locus of expanded human NK cells using CRISPR-SaCas9 ribonucleoprotein electroporation and AAV6 donor-template delivery. We also detail the phenotypic analysis of CAR-NK cells using a 23-marker flow cytometry panel including CAR detection and describe a live-cell imaging assay to evaluate CAR-mediated and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity kinetics.

abstract: Physicochemical testing is a central component of vaccine control because it measures material attributes that can reveal changes in composition, structure, aggregation, particle organization, excipients, and degradation. Its role, however, must be distinguished from immunochemical, cell-based, microbiological, and animal-based tests and must be positioned within an integrated control strategy extending from starting materials and drug substance to in-process controls and the finished product. This narrative review examines physicochemical quality control of prophylactic human vaccines, with emphasis on the Brazilian Pharmacopeia and the United States Pharmacopeia and complementary World Health Organization guidance for selected vaccine categories. General compendial assays are separated from platform-specific tests for protein/subunit, toxoid, polysaccharide/glycoconjugate, viral, and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccines. The literature is synthesized by analytical purpose rather than article-by-article, focusing on chromatography, mass spectrometry, spectroscopy, electrophoretic and particle-analysis methods, stability-indicating characterization, and the relation between critical quality attributes and potency. Advanced methods can improve specificity and mechanistic resolution, but physicochemical integrity alone does not automatically demonstrate biological potency. Their greatest regulatory value is achieved when scientifically relevant attributes are linked to manufacturing consistency, stability, and clinically qualified lots. The review also clarifies how physicochemical methods may support the consistency approach and the 3Rs without conflating them with all in vitro potency assays. Overall, modern vaccine control requires a platform-adapted analytical strategy in which finished-product testing complements, rather than replaces, appropriate drug-substance, in-process, and process-validation controls.

abstract: We describe a DNA-based molecular framework that enables DNA-binding proteins (DBPs) to perform diverse synthetic operations beyond their natural functions. We introduce templated proximity as a mechanism through which DBP-DNA recognition events are converted into programmable DNA strand displacement reactions. In this architecture, protein binding templates the spatial colocalization of split DNA components, generating functional nucleic acid outputs that can be propagated into downstream processes. Using representative DBPs, including EGR1, YY1, and p53, we couple protein recognition to DNA strand displacement, activation of a fluorogenic RNA aptamer, regulation of CRISPR-Cas12a and Cas13 activity, and DBP-triggered activation of hierarchical CRISPR cascades. These results establish templated proximity as a general transduction principle for integrating DNA-binding proteins into modular nucleic acid reaction networks and demonstrate that DBPs can function as programmable interfaces connecting natural biomolecular recognition with engineered DNA-based information processing, enabling modular communication layers with tailored synthetic functionality.

abstract: Amyloidosis comprises a group of systemic disorders caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded precursor proteins, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-related amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) has transitioned from a rare and underdiagnosed condition to a treatable disease, driven by major advances in diagnostic imaging, increased disease awareness, and the approval of disease-modifying therapies. These therapies target transthyretin (TTR) stabilization and amyloid production or deposition and have led to an evolving therapeutic landscape. As therapeutic efficacy is greatest in earlier disease stages, timely recognition is crucial. Effective management of ATTR-CM requires structured screening of high-risk populations, multidisciplinary collaboration, and longitudinal follow-up. This review provides a practical, clinician-focused framework that addresses clinical presentation and "red flags" to facilitate early detection. It offers a comprehensive overview of the diagnostic pathway, including (AI-enabled) electrocardiography analysis, (non-)invasive imaging modalities, biomarkers, and genetic testing. Additionally, emerging therapeutic strategies are discussed, encompassing supportive heart failure management, amyloid-specific treatments such as TTR stabilizers and gene silencers, and novel approaches including fibril depletion and gene-editing therapies. As the therapeutic paradigm shifts from disease stabilization toward potential reversal, early diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies are essential to improve prognosis and quality of life in patients with cardiac amyloidosis.

title: Transforming cardiac amyloidosis care: navigating the evolving diagnostic and therapeutic landscape.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, its 5-year survival rate continues to be unsatisfactory. Current therapies are often limited by resistance, toxicity, or poor efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for novel strategies.
METHOD: We performed a high-throughput compound screen for inducing cell death in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells. Combined with lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release assays, cell death morphology observation, and propidium iodide (PI) staining, we confirmed the cell death mode as pyroptosis. Then, we conducted a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen to identify the critical regulator of compound-induced pyroptosis.
RESULTS: The screening results showed that morusin is a trigger of gasdermin E (GSDME)-mediated pyroptosis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells. Importantly, morusin suppresses tumor growth in vivo. Through a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen, we further demonstrated that angiotensin II receptor type 2 (AGTR2) as a critical regulator of morusin-induced pyroptosis, acting via activation of the caspase-3-GSDME signaling cascade. Notably, morusin also upregulated AGTR2 expression in NSCLC cells. In an NSCLC mouse model, morusin treatment potently suppressed wild-type tumor growth, whereas its antitumor efficacy was substantially diminished in AGTR2-knockout tumors.
CONCLUSION: Our study reveals a novel mechanism underlying the antitumor effect of morusin, establishes AGTR2 as a potential therapeutic target, and provides a rationale for pyroptosis-based therapy for NSCLC.

abstract: The growing recognition of base editing as a precise genome-engineering strategy for single‑nucleotide conversions without double‑strand breaks has increased interest in its application to animal agriculture, where many economically important traits are influenced by single nucleotide variants. Although recent engineering efforts have broadened the targeting scope, improved editing precision, and reduced off‑target activity, major challenges remain in translating these tools to livestock and aquaculture species, particularly with respect to delivery, mosaicism, germline transmission, and breeding-scale deployment. In this review, we outline the development of cytosine, adenine, dual, and mitochondrial base editors, and discuss their advances in livestock and fish, including trait-oriented editing in pigs and cattle, rapid functional validation in model fish, and early proof-of-concept studies in aquaculture species. We further discuss the emerging potential of mitochondrial DNA base editing for animal breeding and evaluate the extent to which current advances support the broader goal of precision breeding and sustainable animal production.

abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) remains a major global health threat, causing recurrent seasonal epidemics and sporadic pandemics. Despite extensive studies on IAV-host interactions, cellular regulation of the viral life cycle is not fully understood. Here, using genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screens, we identified zinc finger FYVE domain-containing protein 21 (ZFYVE21) as a cellular factor required for completion of the IAV life cycle. We show that ZFYVE21 acts upstream of PTEN to maintain endosomal acidification, which triggers the conformational change of viral hemagglutinin (HA) required for membrane fusion and viral uncoating. Deficiency of ZFYVE21 abrogates this acidification step, thereby blocking viral genome release into the cytosol and subsequent replication across multiple IAV strains. Importantly, ZFYVE21-deficient mice exhibit significantly lower lung viral loads, diminished histopathological damage, and markedly improved survival upon lethal IAV H3N2 challenge. Collectively, our findings uncover a critical role of ZFYVE21 in endosomal acidification-dependent IAV genome release into the cytosol and establish ZFYVE21 as a promising target for the development of broad-spectrum anti-influenza therapeutics.

abstract: Phosphatidic acid phosphatases (PAPs) regulate lipid metabolism by controlling the interconversion of phosphatidic acid (PA) and diacylglycerol (DAG), thereby influencing membrane composition and multiple downstream cellular processes. We investigated the role of PAP2-2 in Leishmania mexicana using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene ablation and genetic complementation. Immunofluorescence analyses revealed partial co-localization of PAP2-2 with the endoplasmic reticulum. Ablation of the PAP2-2-encoding gene LmxM.19.1350 significantly reduced total phosphatidic acid phosphatase activity, resulting in marked accumulation of endogenous PA and alterations in lipid composition, including changes in phosphatidylcholine, cardiolipin, sterols, and selected DAG species. PAP2-2-deficient parasites displayed altered cell morphology, reduced growth, and delayed differentiation into metacyclic promastigotes and amastigotes. Furthermore, loss of PAP2-2 impaired mitochondrial physiology, as evidenced by reduced basal respiration, diminished oxidative phosphorylation capacity, altered electron transport chain activities, and decreased responsiveness to respiratory substrates and inhibitors. Our findings identify PAP2-2 as an important regulator of PA/DAG homeostasis in L. mexicana and demonstrate that disruption of this enzyme triggers extensive lipid remodeling with downstream effects on mitochondrial function, parasite development, and cellular morphology. These results highlight the central role of membrane lipid homeostasis in the physiology of Leishmania and establish PAP2-2 as a previously underappreciated determinant of parasite fitness that may represent a promising target for future mechanistic and therapeutic investigations.

abstract: Developing broadly protective influenza vaccines remains a major challenge for global public health. Influenza B viruses cause about one-third of all annual influenza virus infections and current vaccines only show moderate effectiveness against matched virus strains, therefore, development of more effective and broadly protective vaccines against them is important. Chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinin (cHA and mHA) immunogens are under investigation as broadly protective influenza B vaccine candidates. The lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated nucleoside-modified mRNA technology has recently revolutionized vaccination and gained widespread interest due to its successful use in the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. Here, we evaluated influenza B cHA and mHA mRNA-LNP vaccines in non-human primates and compared their immunogenicity to a quadrivalent seasonal influenza virus vaccine. mHA mRNA-LNPs induced high binding antibody titers against antigenically distant influenza B virus strains, with significant hemagglutination inhibition and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity activity and provided protection in mice in a serum transfer challenge experiment. This approach shows great promise for developing broadly protective influenza B vaccines.

abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed a gapmer antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting KCNH1 and evaluated its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and a knock-in mouse model of KCNH1-related disorder. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.

abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most severe manifestation of acute lung injury (ALI), characterized by diffuse pulmonary inflammation, impaired gas exchange, and high morbidity and mortality. Despite the clinical significance of ARDS, no effective pharmacological therapies are currently available. In this study, we developed a lung-targeted mRNA-sulfonium lipid nanoparticle (mRNA/sLNP) delivery system for the treatment of ALI/ARDS in a mouse model. We first examined different heads and tails to optimize sulfonium lipid structure, leading to the identification of a top-performing HOSEH formulation. HOSEH sLNP was comprehensively characterized and subsequently loaded with interleukin-10 (IL-10) mRNA, an immunomodulatory cytokine with potent anti-inflammatory activity. As a proof-of-concept, in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced ALI mouse model, IL-10 mRNA/sLNP demonstrated both prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy, significantly attenuating pulmonary and systemic inflammation, restoring alveolar-capillary barrier integrity, and reducing lung tissue damage. These findings highlight the potential of lung-targeted mRNA therapeutics in inflammatory lung diseases. With further development, IL-10 mRNA/sLNP may represent a promising strategy for the treatment of ALI and ARDS.

abstract: Non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia intermedia (NTDT) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder characterized by decreased β-globin production in erythroid cells resulting from mutations in the β-globin gene that is not treated with transfusion. NTDT is further characterized by a relative excess of α-globin, which drives ineffective erythropoiesis resulting in increased iron absorption and ultimately iron overload. Sapablursen is an antisense oligonucleotide that reduces the production of transmembrane protease serine 6 (TMPRSS6) and increases hepcidin production. This phase 2a study evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of sapablursen in patients with NTDT. Eligible patients had a clinical diagnosis of NTDT with genotypic confirmation of β-globin gene mutations. Twenty-nine patients with NTDT were treated with sapablursen at doses ranging from 30 to 160 mg once every 4 weeks for up to 2 years. Sapablursen was generally safe and well tolerated. The study did not meet its primary or secondary end points of increased blood hemoglobin or reduced liver iron content (LIC). In earlier studies, including a phase 1 trial in healthy volunteers and a phase 2 trial in patients with polycythemia vera, sapablursen produced dose-dependent increases in serum hepcidin levels. However, in patients with NTDT, similar doses and exposures did not lead to consistent dose-dependent increases in serum hepcidin. LIC and serum erythroferrone were elevated at baseline and throughout the current study. These 2 factors may prevent the elevation of serum hepcidin via the TMPRSS6 pathway. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as #NCT04059406.

abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive motor neuron loss. Aberrant RNA metabolism is one of its most consistent molecular features, and ALS has long been framed as a disease of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), given that mutations in RBPs are among the most frequent genetic causes of ALS. However, a growing number of ALS-associated genes encode proteins that lack canonical RNA-binding domains; nonetheless, their mutations also disrupt RNA homeostasis. This review examines how these non-canonical disease modulators perturb RNA metabolism. We group these factors into three functional classes. One includes proteostasis regulators, whose dysfunction impairs protein quality control and promotes the accumulation of aggregation-prone RBPs in cytoplasmic inclusions and persistent stress granules. Another involves factors that elicit RNA toxicity or disrupt ribonucleoprotein organization, including GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9ORF72 and CAG repeat expansion in ATXN1. The third class comprises factors governing axonal RNA granule transport. Across these categories, a shared consequence is the disruption of mRNA processing, stability, localization, and translation in motor neurons. We further discuss how epitranscriptomic dysregulation, particularly altered m6A and m1A modification states, may contribute to ALS pathology. We also discuss the therapeutic implications of this mechanistic convergence in defective RNA metabolism in ALS.

abstract: Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans . We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is FKS1 , encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that fks1 Δ mutants lack β-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

abstract: Gene therapy is one of the breakthrough strategies for treating genetically acquired and complicated disorders owing to its potential in regulating the expression of genes precisely. Nevertheless, the success of any gene therapy will depend upon the development of a safe and efficient system for gene delivery. Nanotechnology has brought about great changes in the field of non-viral gene delivery systems by providing carriers that increase stability, facilitate cellular uptake, allow endosomal escape, and have tissue specificity without causing systemic toxicity. This review examines the basic concepts underlying the design of nanocarriers for the delivery of plasmid DNA, mRNA, siRNA, and the CRISPR-Cas genome editing system. The current review provides an overview of different viral and non-viral delivery platforms for plasmid DNA, mRNA, siRNA, and CRISPR-Cas genome editing systems. The discussion focuses on adenoviral, adeno-associated viral, lentiviral, retroviral, herpes simplex viral and virus-like particle delivery platforms, as well as non-viral nanocarriers. The review further highlights clinically validated examples, such as liposomal nanoparticles used for the delivery of RNA-based therapies and discusses some of the translational challenges that still exist in terms of transfection efficiency, long-term safety issues, manufacturability at a large scale, and regulatory acceptance. Finally, some of the latest trends in gene delivery, such as artificial intelligence-assisted nanoparticle design, smart multi-responsive nanoparticles, and personalized nanomedicine, have been outlined as the most important driving forces in developing the next generation of gene delivery technologies.

abstract: Chronic pulmonary diseases are often associated with high morbidity and/or mortality, and many lack effective therapies. Direct delivery of antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to the lung shows promise for the treatment of pulmonary diseases. Despite their overall low risk profiles, systemically delivered ASOs can be associated with pro-inflammatory responses including activation of the alternative complement pathway, particularly near administration sites. Nonhuman primates (NHPs) and Beagle dogs have both been used in ASO toxicity studies, but comparative suitability of these species for ASO safety assessment has not been established. Herein, we compare the tolerability of a phosphorothioate (PS) gapmer ASO in these species after dosing with a nebulized ASO delivered by inhalation at 15 mg/kg once weekly for 13 weeks via face mask. Although lung concentrations of ASO were similar in cynomolgus monkeys and Beagle dogs, ASO inhalation was associated with greater pro-inflammatory responses in the monkey. Anti-drug antibody production, C-reactive protein elevation, complement activation, increased bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cellularity, increased lung weights, and microscopic evidence of pulmonary inflammation were present in the monkey but not the dog. Therefore, although NHPs and dogs can be used in toxicity testing of inhaled ASOs, NHPs exhibit a predisposition to complement activation and development of pulmonary inflammation.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 620,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli . Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.

abstract: Rare genetic diseases affect over 350 million patients worldwide and have long posed significant challenges in modern medicine. Although messenger RNA (mRNA) was initially considered unsuitable due to its instability, immunogenicity, and inability to cross biological barriers, the COVID-19 pandemic established mRNA as a clinically validated therapeutic. Advances in mRNA synthesis and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) design have since improved stability, translation, safety, and scalability, offering a modern strategy, alongside advances in our understanding of rare diseases. By enabling the production of functional proteins without modifying the genome, mRNA-LNP offer a flexible solution to restore proteins lost through rare genetic diseases. Despite this promise, their application for rare genetic diseases remains at early stages, with most candidates in preclinical developments or early Phase 1/2 trials. This review underlines recent advances in mRNA-based protein replacement for rare genetic disorders, integrating innovations in mRNA design combined with LNPs optimization. It also discusses current challenges, emerging innovations, and future perspectives. While early clinical programs have mainly targeted liver-based disorders, the field is expanding toward pulmonary, hematologic, and neuromuscular diseases. Continued multidisciplinary efforts may establish mRNA nanotherapies as a transformative treatment option for patients with rare genetic disorders.
